title: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims
description: The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands
body: The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands.Sources close to the duchess said Meghan warned Thomas Markle in a letter that he would never meet his grandchildren.It is understood the letter was sent to Markle, 82, while he was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated.It has been reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle had been found in his former home in the Philippines and UK police in 2019 told Meghan about claims of abuse against him. Markle, who is based in the US, denies all such allegations. Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. He pulled out of his daughter's royal wedding that year, citing ill health.The letter sent in 2025 appears to be the end of what has been a troubled relationship between father and daughter.It is understood details of the letter, first reported in the Sun on Sunday, external, include Meghan telling Markle that he would never meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lillibet, with Meghan making it clear she would never contact her father again.She also apparently told her father that authorities were aware of the claims made against him.Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed to the Sun on Friday he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home.He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the US Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) about it in July.The FBI has since confirmed it is aware of the allegations.On Sunday Markle Jnr, 60, apologised to Meghan in an interview with the Sun for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement."I now know I have been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years," he said.Philippines officials have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father, telling the BBC on Friday that its anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force was investigating the matter.Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured Thomas Markle's computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.Meanwhile, Thomas Markle has given an interview to the Mail on Sunday, external in which he acknowledged paying for sex in the Philippines on past visits but denies sleeping with underage girls and ever possessing child abuse images.

schema.headline: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims

title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
description: The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.Spe
body: The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said he wants to pursue a new type of relationship with Brussels, potentially including full EU membership or joining the single market, which would require free movement."I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the newspaper.Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said there could be "no return" to free movement after the 2016 EU referendum, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the prime minister's comments were a betrayal of voters who supported Brexit.Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.He has said that any fundamental changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the "leave" campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.But the prime minister suggested the type of migration experienced during the years of EU membership was "different" from the challenges faced now."It was generally younger people, not always, but spending a few years, then going back," he said in his told the Sunday Times., external"And obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well."He acknowledged that freedom of movement "had very significant challenges associated with it"."Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said."The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."Burnham's willingness to re-open some of the most sensitive debates in British politics has been a feature of his first months in power.In an interview with the BBC in September, Burnham said Britain could go "all the way" towards rejoining the European Union.However, in his latest remarks, the prime minister stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. While the UK did not previously abandon the pound while it was an EU member, the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the single currency.The remarks were made ahead of his meeting with EU chiefs at a summit on 20 November in Brussels, where he is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.The shadow home secretary said EU free movement would amount to "handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe".Philp said: "The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it."Burnham won the Greater Manchester seat of Makerfield at a by-election in June, ahead of him becoming prime minister the following month. The constituency voted to leave the European Union in 2016.As a candidate in the by-election, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".In response to the Sunday Times interview, Farage said: "This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch"."He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty," the Reform UK leader added.

schema.headline: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement

title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
description: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentWe're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.That is the cash buffer the gove
body: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentWe're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around £24bn to as low as £11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.Increasing taxes on capital gains or extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor to raise some more money, external on Wednesday.1. Increase taxes on banksBanks in the UK have seen profits rise in recent years because they have been able to charge people higher interest rates when borrowing money.And there is widespread belief among bank bosses that the chancellor is preparing to raise taxes on banks in this week's Budget.Think tank Tax Policy Associates estimates, external that increasing the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax from 3% to 5.5% could potentially raise an additional £1bn to £2bn a year for the Treasury.2. Higher taxes on gambling machinesFormer Prime Minister Gordon Brown has called on Healey to hike the tax on electronic gaming machines - such as those found in betting shops and adult gaming centres which can offer payouts of £500 per game - citing the social harm imposed by problem gambling.The Social Market Foundation (SMF) think tank has estimated, external that doubling tax on these machines from 20% to 40% could raise could raise between £275m and £460m - depending on how gamblers reacted to it.People who use gambling machines could also end up having the tax passed on to them through worse odds on games, though anti-gambling groups argue this could help discourage more people from using them.Research from the SMF found that gambling machines are increasingly clustered on some of the UK's most deprived high streets, and that one in four people who play casino games on these machines gamble at risky or harmful levels.3. Get online marketplaces to collect VATReports suggest the chancellor is preparing to announce that big online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by retailers selling on their platforms.The Treasury estimates it is missing out on around £12bn a year, external in VAT revenues that should be paid by companies, which it calls the "VAT tax gap".Tax experts say that part of the problem - although not accounting for the full £12bn of the VAT gap - is that some online sellers fail to comply with VAT rules, either by not charging VAT when they should or by failing to pass on VAT collected from customers to the government.Enforcement can be difficult because some firms that use platforms like Amazon to sell their products are based overseas and falsely present themselves as UK-established businesses.Others close down and reopen under different company names to escape their tax liabilities.Reports suggest that this move to make big online marketplaces responsible for collecting the tax - rather than the individual retailers - would clamp down on this form of tax evasion and could raise around £1bn in extra VAT a year.Amazon, which supports the move, has estimated it could raise £700m, external a year in VAT for the government.Some sellers could respond by raising prices or leaving the platform, which could have an impact on some shoppers.However, it would also level the playing field for online sellers, ensuring those businesses who charge VAT are not illegally undercut by those who break the rules and do not.4. Cut welfare spendingThe above three tax measures together would raise a maximum of only around £3.5bn a year.That would be small relative to the sums of money the chancellor might well need to restore his headroom and pay for any new spending.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in the summer he wanted a "fair and lasting" reduction to the UK's welfare bill, while the government is under pressure from opposition parties to find savings from working-age benefits.The Conservatives claim they could make savings of £36bn a year by restricting people's access to welfare payments.Reform say they would save £50bn a year in this way, although independent analysts say there are questions about how realistic it is to make such large savings.Working health and sickness benefits have risen sharply since the Covid pandemic and the overall cost is projected by the Office for Budget Responsibility to increase from £68bn this year to £81bn in 2031.Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves attempted to reduce spending on these benefits , externalby £5bn a year by 2030, but were forced to reverse course after a revolt by backbench Labour MPs.Independent welfare experts and economists say savings from the working age welfare budget are possible but would likely require upfront spending to help people into work, which could cancel out any near-term savings for the Treasury.Cuts to health and disability welfare would reduce the incomes of people who currently receive those payments, external and/or those who would otherwise receive them in future - and campaigners warn of the risk of people being pushed into poverty.However, if more welfare claimants were also supported into work, their overall incomes could be maintained or even rise.Graphics by Callum Thomson and Lewis McBlane.

schema.headline: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax

title: Music streaming: Why we're listening to so many old songs
description: Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlistsImage source, Getty Images for iHeartRadioImage caption, One of 2026's biggest hits is
body: Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlistsImage source, Getty Images for iHeartRadioImage caption, One of 2026's biggest hits is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, originally released in 2015ByThomas SpencerMore music is being created than at any other time in human history. Every day, more than 100,000 songs, external are being submitted to streaming services. And despite the deluge of AI music, external - Spotify says it has removed 75 million "spammy tracks" from its catalogue - real music still makes up most of our listening. The streaming service Deezer says AI accounts for just 0.5% of streams on its platform.The problem for all those artists creating new music is that our listening habits increasingly show a love for nostalgia.Luminate, an independent entertainment data and analytics company that tracks music, film, and television consumption first started tracking music streaming in 2008.This year, it recorded that the streaming of current music (released less than 18 months ago) was significantly dwarfed by older music in both the UK and US.In the first half of 2026, almost two thirds of the music played (about 60%) was released five or more years ago.So, if we're stuck in a streaming rut, what's to blame?Old vs new?In the UK, most of us seem to be shunning new songs.Eighteen of the year's top 20 bestselling songs, external were released 12 months ago, or earlier. The year's eighth biggest hit is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, which originally came out in June 2015. Michael Jackson's Billie Jean (1983) is in 22nd place. Fleetwood Mac's Dreams (1977) is 30th.It's a sign that, with practically every song ever recorded available at the press of a button, people are increasingly seeking out the classics - or what the music industry categorises as "deep catalogue".It's a similar story in the US.There, in the two most-played genres, R&B and Hip-Hop, external, about 60% of streams are old-school catalogue hits.A 'drought' of new music in the UK Charts?Even when current songs do break out, they themselves dominate streaming for weeks and even months.Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's duet Rein Me In recently made UK chart history, spending a record-breaking 23 non-consecutive weeks at number one.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Olivia Dean and Sam Fender have broken chart history with Rein Me In, after 19 non-consecutive weeks at the top of the UK singles chartWhat about grassroots music?Even after a song has gone viral, some musicians say it can be hard to promote subsequent releases and sustain a career. A platform like TikTok isn't set up to boost artists, it's there to create viral moments around a single song."It's easier [today] for folks to be passive fans," noted J Erving, the founder of Raye's distribution company, Human Re Sources, in a recent interview with Billboard, external. "For you to consider yourself broken [as a mainstream artist], people need to care about you beyond the song. Where is the connectivity? Are people really dialled in in a deeper way?" It's a problem the music industry is keen to tackle.Oliver Schusser, the Head of Apple Music, says his streaming service is working to champion "tomorrow's artists" in its curation."You know, we do the Super Bowl halftime show, we need to make sure that we still have performers in 10, 20, 30 years," he tells BBC News. "Because if you look back at the performers we had in the last four years, they all started somewhere before they got to the world's biggest stage."Other organisations like Sofar Sounds work exclusively with grassroots musicians, putting on intimate pop-up gigs in cities across the globe.This October, its Shoreditch Sofar Fringe festival showcased a whole host of artists like East London rapper J Casa.Image source, J CasaImage caption, Rapper J Casa is one of thousands of grassroots artists trying to cut through the noise on streaming platformsIn an age of content oversaturation, Casa thinks there's something unique about a live performance.Rather than hearing more of what they already know, Casa says audiences form "a lasting connection" with a new artist and their music.Sofar is also launching its Human Discovery Movement, external campaign that aims to put music curation and discovery "back into human hands."Music lovers can now text a "mystery number" and receive voice notes from Sofar's tastemakers with recommendations for new music worldwide.Are streaming platforms preaching to the choir?Artificial intelligence (AI) may also be playing its part in the so-called death of new music.Spotify, and its competitors like Apple Music and Amazon Music, are driving the trend in AI-assisted curation, allowing premium subscribers to automatically generate playlists through text prompts to fit a mood, vibe or occasion.Musicologist Anna-Kaisa Kaila thinks "there absolutely is potential for bias" with AI-generative playlist technology."With AI systems, the bias can either come from the data or from the system itself. If there's not enough training data in a particular style that is perhaps not so commercially dominant, it will be that much harder for the system to pull up tracks in that style."Others fear an algorithmic streaming bubble is to the detriment of genuine music, its discovery and creatives' livelihoods.As Tim Garcia, London-based DJ and curator puts it: "They're based on everyone's listening behaviour and data, right? So, you're probably going to get given a very similar recommendation to an artist you're already listening to."Dan Mackta, managing director at Qobuz, an online music platform that maintains a strict human-first approach to curation, agrees the technology "is never going to want to throw a curve ball at you".Image source, Jordan MatykaImage caption, London-based artist Chiminyo performs at his ongoing jazz-electronic NRG projectChiminyo, a London-based independent artist, believes that auto-generated playlists are also misleading people into thinking they're listening to "hand-picked" tunes from bona fide artists - as opposed to digitally mass-produced sound-alikes created to catch streams.Scrolling through a "relaxing jazz piano playlist" with over 370,000 saves on Spotify, he spots that top featured artists that rack up hundreds of thousands of monthly listens have unverified accounts.Little - if anything - can be found about them online, he says.To his trained ear, Chiminyo also says the different artists' tracks sound near identical, reason enough to conclude the compositions have been synthetically mass-produced."Its all the same: the same piano feel, the same microphone placement, the same tape machine, has been used on every single one of these tracks."When asked, Spotify said it had rolled out platform-wide policies, external against impersonation and is working to the improve filtering out of AI-related issues on its platform. But it acknowledges AI's use in music production sits on a spectrum with some artists choosing to use it to varying degrees.New music may not be dying out, but it's clear it has a lot to contend with in 2026.

schema.headline: Music streaming: Why we're listening to so many old songs

title: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates
description: All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred f
body: All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred from entering all settlements.The restrictions come amid a crackdown in the occupied West Bank after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the territory.The Israel Defense Forces announced a "ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings" on Tuesday.It said most workers would also be barred from settlements from Sunday, with the exception of industrial zones and a limited number of other areas.Before the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, more than 100,000 Palestinian workers were permitted to enter Israel. Since then only a small fraction have had their permits restored.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a major operation on Friday in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.The Israeli military have been demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron, with hundreds of families having been displaced. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 residents had been displaced by the operation, which has led to at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened, according to footage shared online.Even before the entry and exit bans on workers were announced by the IDF on Sunday, the military had cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, just days ahead of Israel's election taking place on Tuesday.In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, Netanyahu threatened a "very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory.Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said the operation was being "driven by the elections" and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far right and the settlers.On Saturday, thousands gathered in Tel Aviv for a large anti-government demonstration.The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of victims and hostages taken by militants on 7 October 2023, to demand accountability for the failure to prevent the Hamas-led attack."Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability, and establish a state commission of inquiry," the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.The gathering saw the participation of the leaders of the four main opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff who is neck and neck with Netanyahu.

schema.headline: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates

title: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents
description: Image source, Eddie LeverImage caption, Eddie Lever was able to leave his tenancy more easily because of the Renters' Rights ActByBecky MortonPolitica
body: Image source, Eddie LeverImage caption, Eddie Lever was able to leave his tenancy more easily because of the Renters' Rights ActByBecky MortonPolitical reporterWhen the Renters' Rights Act came into force in May it was described as the biggest change for tenants in England in a generation, giving more stability and security to the millions of people who rent from private landlords.The legislation has also prompted a shake-up of the student rental market, which has posed challenges for landlords as it allows people to leave a tenancy rather than being tied in for the full academic year.Eddie Lever had finished his first year at the University of Exeter when he decided the course wasn't for him.The 20-year-old wanted to switch to studying international relations at the University of York but had already organised his house for the upcoming year.The tenancy was signed and had started.But because of changes in the Renters' Rights Act, Eddie only had to give two months' notice before he could leave and stop paying rent.The legislation ended fixed-term tenancies - where renters are tied in to contracts for a specific number of months. For students, previously contracts were generally for the full academic year.Instead, properties are now rented on a rolling basis, which means tenants pay rent weekly or monthly with no fixed end date.University-owned halls of residence and Purpose-Built Student Accommodation are exempt, external and can still offer fixed-term contracts so this change primarily affects students renting from a private landlord."If the Renters' Rights Act wasn't a thing, I don't think I would have been able to move universities because I would have been locked into the full [year] contract," Eddie explains."It would have made it unaffordable."As he was signed up to a joint tenancy, when he left it ended the tenancy for the whole house.Fortunately, Eddie had a friend who was looking for a room who was able to take his place so his housemates could sign a new tenancy.He acknowledges the situation would have been more difficult for his housemates if there wasn't someone who could take his room.However, Eddie thinks the benefits for students are worth this risk."If you were to fall out with your flatmates or if you decide that university is not for you, being locked into a full-term contract can be really prohibitive financially," he says."So without that flexibility, people can really be locked into situations that they don't necessarily want to be in."Lewis Wilson, vice president for higher education at the National Union of Students, says this flexibility means students can also save money on rent by moving home for the summer.While previously, many student rental contracts ran into the summer after courses had finished, students can now choose to move out earlier if they want.Wilson says students also benefit from wider changes in the act, which bans landlords in England from evicting tenants without a reason.Campaigners argue this gives renters greater security and confidence to ask for repairs, without fearing they could be evicted if they raise concerns.Image source, NUSImage caption, Lewis Wilson from the NUS says the legislation has given students more freedom to move out when they wantHowever, greater flexibility for students to leave tenancies also means less certainty for landlords.The act did introduce a specific ground, external for landlords to evict a group of students at the end of the academic year if they intend to re-let the property to students.Chris Norris, chief policy officer at the National Residential Landlords Association, says the bigger problem for student landlords is if their tenants choose to move out earlier.He argues this is a bigger risk for students - who may fall out with their housemates or drop out of university - than, for example, families, who are less likely to want to move out after just a few months.Norris says the end of fixed-term tenancies means student houses could be left empty over the summer after courses finish - or even earlier.He adds that it is now more difficult for student landlords to rent a house for just a few months as they don't know how long the tenants will stay and can't guarantee it will be available for students again in the autumn.Norris says it's early days for the new legislation and many landlords are taking this year as a test to see how these issues play out in practice.However, he warns that some may choose to increase the monthly rent they charge to cover the risk of their properties being empty over the summer.In some cases, he says landlords may even sell up or stop renting to students, reducing supply and pushing up prices.Image source, Sue LawesImage caption, Sue Lawes thinks the changes mean many student landlords will put up their rentSue Lawes, who rents three shared houses to students in Norwich, is worried about the changes.While Sue says she doesn't want to put up her prices, if her houses end up being empty over the summer because students decide to end their tenancy after their final exams she says she may have to.She has already brought forward the start of her tenancy agreements to August instead of September to try and reduce the risks of this.However, she says if her tenants move out earlier in the year she would struggle to make a profit, whilst covering costs including her mortgage, council tax and utility standing charges when the properties are empty.She argues higher monthly rents would mean bigger upfront costs for students and higher overall costs for those who do choose to carry on renting over the summer.Sue stresses that she supports the aim of the legislation to give tenants greater security and that students should be able to move out if their landlord is not carrying out repairs.But she wants landlords to be allowed to offer fixed-term contracts to students in line with the academic year to avoid properties being left empty over the summer."Landlords are going to find it very, very hard to absorb those void periods," she says."Landlords will put prices up and students are going to pay."

schema.headline: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents

title: Budget to include £1bn for social and affordable housing
description: More than £1bn for social and affordable housing in England will be provided in the Budget, taking funding for the government's 10-year homes programm
body: More than £1bn for social and affordable housing in England will be provided in the Budget, taking funding for the government's 10-year homes programme past £40bn.Mayors and regional leaders across England are also expected to get greater powers and funding in Wednesday's announcement - with councils helped to borrow money from the government to invest in housebuilding through  preferential interest rates.It is hoped the plans will give regional leaders more flexibility and authority over investment decisions.Chancellor John Healey said English cities and regions would get the "right to decide their own future", while Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the plans were about shifting power to those "who know their communities best". The chancellor will also announce more support for small breweries, with the Treasury saying he wants "to turn the tide for our pint producers".Meanwhile, the Sunday Times reports, external that Healey is expected to unveil billions of pounds of new defence spending in the Budget. Specific details on the funding would be outlined at next year's spending reviewBut shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has called for Healey to resign if he fails to set out how the UK will spend 3% of the UK's GDP on defence by 2030.Under the plans for the regions, an initial £285m in transitional seed funding will be allocated by the government next year to support mayors and local leaders - and reduce reliance on "fragmented bidding pots" in Whitehall, the Treasury said.The government will also confirm that it will work with mayors to design a new £1.5bn borrowing facility from 2028, which would allow them to access capital needed to support local priorities.The Treasury said this could be put towards new homes, bringing high streets back to life, or improving transport links.Healey said: "Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas."Areas across the country which are not yet strategic authorities will be able to access a share of the £285m funding to "unlock projects which will contribute to growth in their areas".The prime minister said: "I'm calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country."Claire Ward, chairwoman of the UK Mayors Network and Labour's East Midlands mayor, said that having the "right powers and resources through increased devolution" would help turn "ambitious plans into reality and deliver real, lasting change" for communities.Lord Sadiq Khan, Labour's mayor of London, said greater ability to invest could "help unlock transformational infrastructure projects" including the West London Orbital route, the extension of the Bakerloo Underground line and Docklands Light Railway, and the development of Stratford International station.However, Healey's Budget preparations suffered a blow when the Treasury's entrepreneurship adviser, Alex Depledge, announced she was resigning from the role. She will leave on Thursday, the day after the Budget.Start-ups, she told the Sunday Times, external, were being treated as a "sideshow" and should not be pushed to the "margins of economic policy"."Keeping scale-ups on the fringes underestimates the contribution of our greatest companies, and we need to support and develop them on British shores at all costs," she said.Leading up to the Budget, defence has also remained a key talking point. Healey resigned in June from his role as defence secretary in the previous government over the defence investment plan, which he claimed fell "well short" of what was needed to fund the armed forces.He had called for defence spending to rise to 3% of the country's GDP by 2030, on the way to reaching a Nato target of 3.5% in 2035.But urging him to commit to setting out plans to spend 3% of GDP on defence, the shadow chancellor said: "We are living in an era of extraordinary threats, and yet the chancellor is dithering over finding the money to pay the country's insurance premium... you cannot have a strong economy without a strong defence".Responding to Andrew Griffith's comments, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Conservatives were to blame for failing to invest in the military while in office.Streeting said the prime minister had made it clear that his government was "determined to give our armed forces the investment needed to keep us safe".

schema.headline: Budget to include £1bn for social and affordable housing

title: Bukangi: Will the shark leave the Busan canal and make it back to sea?
description: A shark went astray and captured Korea's heart - will she finally make it back to sea?Figure caption, Watch: BBC follows operation to rescue shark str
body: A shark went astray and captured Korea's heart - will she finally make it back to sea?Figure caption, Watch: BBC follows operation to rescue shark stranded in South Korean canalByJake KwonSeoul correspondent Reporting fromBusan, South KoreaAs soon as a large shark was spotted in a canal in Busan - a bustling shipping hub and beach city on South Korea's south-eastern tip - marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo was drafted in to rescue it. He got the call in mid-September, on his way home from a business trip tracking shoals of mackerel to aid fishing vessels. Despite being one of the country's leading shark experts, he never thought he'd be asked by the coastguard to actually save one.South Korea is no stranger to sharks but one this size, in a shallow, concrete canal right by the world's seventh busiest port, was unheard of - until now.With an excited crowd already gathering at the waterfront, his team from the National Institute of Fisheries Science had to move fast.The first task was to determine the species.Some sharks are more dangerous than others. The star of the 1975 blockbuster Jaws, the great white shark, is known to attack and kill humans. The specimen in Busan was found to be a female dusky shark, a species linked only to two deadly attacks. Still, Kim feared someone in the crowd might jump or fall into the canal. The shark had to return to sea.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The dusky shark was first spotted in the canal in mid-September A small coastguard ship made an initial attempt using an electrical deterrence device, which generates a weak current that sharks avoid. They're usually used after sightings near popular beaches. But after five hours, officials determined this particular shark was too large and fast for the device.Kim changed tack, deciding instead to wait for the shark to let herself out. But that did not happen.As authorities looked for ways to guide her out of the canal, the stranded creature went viral.Just hours after she appeared, the council had sent everyone in the city an emergency text alert, urging pedestrians and residents to "exercise caution for their safety".People rarely visited the park along the canal but because of the message, the place was soon brimming with people eager to spot the shark.Adoring fans named her Bukangi, from "buk hang", the Korean name of the nearby harbour. Within days, a business trademarked it and Bukangi pins, plushies and T-shirts began selling online. City authorities joined in, livestreaming the shark and making her their official mascot. A banner was hung at the entrance of the canal, asking the public to sign a petition "on behalf of Bukangi" to demand the national government's support for the construction of a new 30,000-seater baseball stadium by the canal.Shark spotting became a team effort among locals and visitors. The unspoken rule was that children were given the front row, and whoever saw Bukangi had to point her out to newer arrivals. Some self-appointed defenders even patrolled the canal at night to make sure no-one was shining torches or lasers at Bukangi.Image source, Hosu Lee/BBCImage caption, A poster encourages support for a baseball stadium "on behalf of Bukangi"More than 1.6 million visitors ultimately flocked to the canal.The local mayor said the shark brought "the kind of publicity even billions of dollars cannot buy" to the port."It's really rare these days for people to come together," said Kim Joo-eun, who came to see the shark with her two nieces. "I feel that Bukangi brought us all together, cheering for her… It's a lot of fun."But officials couldn't leave Bukangi in the canal.As September drew to an end, she hadn't been seen feeding for days and was spotted with bloody abrasions on her snout from bumping into the concrete walls.Prominent marine biology professor Choi Yoon told local media that experts were particularly worried about a "critical" injury around the shark's eye.Image source, Hosu Lee/BBCImage caption, Kim Joo-eun and her nieces were among Bukangi's many visitorsAt the end of September, Kim's team mounted another rescue attempt. The marine biologist looked back to a 2004 incident in Massachusetts, when water jets were used to drive a great white shark away from a shallow pond.But when the team tried this on Bukangi, she kept circling back.On 2 October, they decided to install a net spanning the width of the canal to stop her from returning. She managed to swim around the net and was back within hours.At this point, Kim started thinking the shark might have problems with her snout's electromagnetic sensors, which she uses for navigation. Or she might have become confused by the loud noises emitted by ships in the harbour.The reason Bukangi was even in the canal may be a sign of warming seas, the oceans ministry suggests. It believes she may have followed plentiful fish to warmer waters. Some 50 large sharks were recorded off South Korea's east coast in the first half of the year; four times as many as last year.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The canal leading up to the Busan port where Bukangi was strandedWith each failed attempt some of Bukangi's newfound fans began demanding she be left in peace. On Thursday, several showed up with placards and shouted "leave Bukangi alone" and "remove the net".When a security guard told them to stop, one man cried: "I love you, Bukangi!""I am obsessed with her," said Jeong Yo-won, a woman in her 40s. She called the shark a "source of hope and joy" and insisted, "I don't think we should evict her mercilessly like this."Image source, Hosu Lee/BBCImage caption, Jeong protesting against Bukangi's "eviction", alongside a man demanding officials "protect Bukangi's right to self-determination" Others thought it was time for her to return home. "I would stare at her for hours because I was so enamoured by her," a woman said after sighting the shark on her third attempt. "I hope Bukangi would stay, but I prefer that she lives a long and healthy life."People joked the council should "make an official ID for Bukangi and give a pension", Shin Seungmin said."She brought so much fun with her. But she should go and live her normal shark life."Image source, Hosu Lee/BBCImage caption, Bukangi became a sensation, drawing the curious and the concerned  Staying in the canal would seriously jeopardise Bukangi because of falling autumn temperatures, Kim explains. Usually this prompts sharks to migrate to warmer waters further south."This canal is far from something we can call a habitat," he adds. "A wild animal cannot stay in a space made strictly for humans."Eventually, as public scrutiny grew, the oceans ministry took over the rescue operation from the fisheries institute. Around 40 personnel, including divers from Busan's aquarium, were mobilised. A vet was on standby, along with an ambulance in case the divers were attacked by Bukangi. On Wednesday divers installed two layers of nets, and Bukangi was successfully herded out of the narrow canal into open water. But overnight, she swam back into the canal, diving under the outer net.This left her trapped between the two layers.Then on thursday, rescuers removed the outer layer, and Bukangi was seen swimming further and further towards open sea.Although she did occasionally circle back, the rescue operation had ended.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Staying in the canal is dangerous for Bukangi, says marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo There have been no sightings of Bukangi in the last few days, which experts say is a positive sign. Prof Choi believes she may be adjusting to wider, deeper waters. She is unlikely to have travelled far, he adds, and could reappear over the coming week.But he is also worried about any injuries she may have sustained. Trapped in the canal, it "kept scraping against [the walls], stripping the skin off its snout and even its pectoral fins", he told local media. For now, South Korea is holding its breath, hoping Bukangi can find her way back to her home - the open sea. Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi in Seoul

schema.headline: Bukangi: Will the shark leave the Busan canal and make it back to sea?

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Cops didn't share letter' and Burnham 'open' to EU free movement
description: A number of the front pages report what they believe will be in Wednesday's Budget. The Sunday Telegraph says the chancellor is considering a carbon c
body: A number of the front pages report what they believe will be in Wednesday's Budget. The Sunday Telegraph says the chancellor is considering a carbon charge on imported fuel., external The paper calls it a "green tax" and claims the move could drive up prices at the pumps. The Sunday Times says there'll be billions of pounds of new funding for defence, external - and two government investment funds will also receive money, which will be invested in UK defence firms.The Sunday Mirror welcomes news of £1bn being committed to council and affordable, external housing, equivalent to building 10,000 thousand homes. It says the government also plans to help more councils borrow to construct homes by extending preferential rates. The paper's editorial says Britain will be a happier place when everyone has a secure roof over their heads.The Sunday Express features a call for the government to reveal whether or not it intends to bring forward the planned rise, external in the state pension age to 68. The paper says there are concerns it could be implemented in 2037, and not the mid-2040s - as originally planned.In an interview with the Observer, the co-founder of Microsoft, Bill Gates, calls the advent of artificial intelligence an "evolutionary event", external. He says people will no longer be the most intelligent things on the planet. He says governments will need to find new sources of income to fund the needs of people put out of work. Gates also says that billionaires should pay more tax, claiming he would have paid more than double the amount he has so far in his life.The Sun on Sunday has been told, by a friend of the Duchess of Sussex,, external that she is "concerned" that the Met police did not act on a letter accusing her estranged father Thomas Markle, of child sexual abuse. "They had the opportunity to pass it on to other relevant law enforcement authorities but chose not to", the friend said. In an interview with the Mail on Sunday, Markle denies all of the allegations, external made against him. Markle, who had a leg amputated last year, tells the paper: "I am not well enough to go to the Philippines but I will speak to anyone who wants to talk to me. I have nothing to hide."Wind-up radios are selling out, after the government's emergency stockpiling announcement, according to the Sunday Telegraph. It says sales increased fivefold at some retailers, external. An industry source revealed that some shops were surprised by the announcement that people should make sure they have three days' worth of food and water - just a day after a worldwide scramble to fix vulnerabilities in the software which underpins the internet. One business owner has told the paper: "I thought my phone was glitching or had been hacked when I saw the number of orders coming in."

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Cops didn't share letter' and Burnham 'open' to EU free movement

title: Liverpool: Why are Andoni Iraola's side struggling for goals in the Premier League?
description: It is a small sample size and still so early in the Premier League season, but notable that in Liverpool's seven matches so far they have scored just
body: It is a small sample size and still so early in the Premier League season, but notable that in Liverpool's seven matches so far they have scored just nine goals. That is in stark contrast to high-flying Brighton, who have already scored 23 top-flight goals and visit Anfield on Sunday, where Liverpool are awaiting their first home win in the Premier League under Andoni Iraola.Across three Champions League games and a Carabao Cup tie against Tottenham, Iraola's side have been the entertainers, scoring 15 goals. Even after the departure of Mohamed Salah Liverpool have plenty of goals in them, and that is evidenced by having 10 different goalscorers already this campaign.So why are they averaging 3.75 goals per game outside the Premier League, as opposed to just 1.29 goals per game in it?Iraola was asked if he knew why, after Liverpool scored four against Villarreal at Anfield on Tuesday, less than a week after they put six past LASK in Austria."I don't really know the reason," he said. "It's true that the LASK game is different but against Villarreal and Atletico Madrid, I think we've been offensively, especially, really good. "In the Premier League, we are not scoring at this level and also we are probably defending better. "They are different kind of games and different kind of opposition, I think more than [the difference being] the competitions, it is who you have played against."Iraola's side are definitely defending better in the Premier League, with three clean sheets and eight goals conceded, compared to eight conceded in four games in the Champions League and Carabao Cup.But Liverpool have conceded first in four of those seven league games and naturally that makes it tougher to break teams down, particularly if the opposition set up into a low block.Iraola's indication that it is more to do with the style of the teams they're facing is interesting.In his first press conference as Liverpool boss, he was asked by BBC Sport about the importance of his core principles. In Arne Slot's second season Liverpool constantly failed to get through low blocks but Iraola suggested he preferred that approach from the opposition."I prefer to face low blocks in terms of the way we will be in control of the games - probably we will concede less chances and spend a lot of time in the opposition half," former Bournemouth manager Iraola said in July."Some teams give you that situation straight away. Other teams do not give you that situation straightaway because they will try to control the game and play in your half."I am looking forward to spending as much time inside the opposition half - with the ball and without the ball - because I feel we are closer to scoring from that position."Liverpool have faced a low block in 28% of their games - more than any other Premier League side - while the 15% of their games facing a high block is the fewest.Clearly, a number teams prefer to set up against Liverpool with a low block and Iraola is realising the reality of it is slightly different - but now it is about breaking through and they have made an array of signings, with the intention of doing just that. "You have more moments of technical brilliance in European football so the players they [Liverpool] have recruited don't have to adapt to that level but are probably around the elite of that level," a current analyst for a Champions League team says."That results in more chances and more goals but the Premier League is completely different. Iraola's style benefits from having the space to attack and we saw that at Bournemouth," the analyst adds.One of the main reasons for bringing Iraola in was to deliver a front-foot style of football, and blessed with attacking quality from the likes of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola, Cody Gakpo, Victor Munoz and Rio Ngumoha, the expectation for more is clear.The xG table suggests that Liverpool should have scored 10.9 goals in the league. Before this weekend, eight teams - including newly promoted Ipswich and struggling Manchester United - have scored more than the Reds.In mitigation, it's worth noting that Arsenal have scored 11 Premier League goals this season and won the league in 2025-26 with an average of 1.87 goals per game.With Liverpool's next league games coming up against Brighton, who won’t be afraid to try and control the game, and the reigning champions in Arsenal, Iraola will be hoping that his attack can click and deliver a statement performance.

schema.headline: Liverpool: Why are Andoni Iraola's side struggling for goals in the Premier League?

title: Clayface's Tom Rhys Harries says prosthetics helped performance
description: Actors are often said to be the face of the film, but in Tom Rhys Harries' breakout role in DC's latest blockbuster, that part of the body becomes the
body: Actors are often said to be the face of the film, but in Tom Rhys Harries' breakout role in DC's latest blockbuster, that part of the body becomes the focal point to chart the character's descent into villainy.Rhys Harries plays the lead in Clayface as Matt Hagen - a handsome, successful actor.When his face is mutilated in an attack, he volunteers for trials of a new treatment with horrifying side effects that transform his face into living clay.The Welsh actor said he spent about half of his time on the set with the special effects make-up team, transforming into the mutant villain.Despite the difficulty of wearing extensive prosthetics during filming, Rhys Harries said it helped him portray the distress of his character in a film that has been described as a body horror psychological thriller."There was a benefit to having it, because the character is in discomfort," he said.Clayface first appeared in DC comics in 1940 as a Batman villain, however the character has never been adapted for cinema, until now, and it is the first major studio movie role for Rhys Harries.

schema.headline: Clayface's Tom Rhys Harries says prosthetics helped performance

title: GTA 6: Can you cheat on someone with a video game character?
description: 'It gives me the ick': Can you cheat on someone with a video game?Image source, Rockstar gamesImage caption, The relationship between the two main cha
body: 'It gives me the ick': Can you cheat on someone with a video game?Image source, Rockstar gamesImage caption, The relationship between the two main characters, Jason and Lucia, is at the centre of Rockstar's latest Grand Theft Auto titleByJim ReedHealth reporterImagine your partner spending hours flirting with someone else, trying to hold their hand and taking them on dates. Most people would have questions.But what if that someone only exists inside a video game?The latest instalment in Rockstar's blockbuster Grand Theft Auto franchise is set to be the biggest entertainment launch of the year when it is released next month.Judging by previews, the connection between its two main characters is a central feature.Rockstar has hinted that the Bonnie and Clyde-type protagonists Jason and Lucia do not have to become a full-on romantic couple.But their relationship can grow by spending time together outside of the main crime and life-on-the-run storyline – through shopping, visiting bars and restaurants and working out together.Smaller interactions like holding hands and quickly responding to each other's texts can help build a bond.The idea has restarted a debate almost as old as gaming itself: if you are that invested in a fictional relationship, is your real-life partner entitled to be upset?In September, polling company YouGov put that question to more than 4,000 British adults.About 6% said they would regard it as cheating, while a further 19% said they would "not be okay with it". Women were considerably more likely than men to take a dim view.Alli Franco, a 30-year-old Texan who posts anime and gaming content to more than a million followers, external on TikTok, says she felt "dismayed" watching the debate unfold online."If your partner is insecure about a fictional character, then there needs to be some serious reflection," she told the BBC."It's similar to having a crush on a TV star, but even further removed from cheating since there is no other actual person involved.”After Franco posted a video on the subject, hundreds of commenters appeared to agree with her, although some did have reservations."To be honest, it depends," wrote one. "If you're cancelling plans with your significant other or directing your intimacy towards a fictional character, then that is a little odd.""It's very odd and it really gives me the ick," one woman told us.Figure caption, Can you cheat on your partner in a video game character?Mimicking social relationshipsFor decades, video games have allowed players to build relationships with non-player characters, or NPCs.Gamers could marry villagers in Harvest Moon in 1996, shape emotional storylines in Final Fantasy VII and pursue more complex romances in role-playing games like Baldur's Gate II.In life simulator The Sims, they could flirt, date, marry and have children with computer-controlled characters.But all those interactions were tightly scripted, based on rules and storylines written in advance by game developers.GTA 6 appears to offer something more dynamic, allowing players to shape the relationship between Jason and Lucia through a wider range of open-world interactions and choices."The more sophisticated games get, the less likely it is that players get pulled out of the experience," says Arienne Ferchaud, an associate professor at Florida State University who studies how people form connections with fictional characters."Games are doing a better job of mimicking reality and mimicking social relationships."Image source, Rockstar gamesImage caption, Rockstar has said players do not have to build a romantic connection in the gameGrand Theft Auto 6 may represent the current cutting edge of game design, but the next leap forward could come from artificial intelligence.Nvidia, Ubisoft and other huge tech companies are already experimenting with generative AI systems that allow players to hold more natural conversations with NPCs.Future characters could remember past encounters, react to a player's actions and build relationships that change over time rather than following a pre-written script.Ferchaud believes that could make games feel even more immersive."You could have relationships that feel more solid or more special," she says, although she argues AI as it exists today would still be creating "a stronger illusion" rather than a genuinely meaningful connection.Whether that is exciting or unsettling may depend on the player, and there has been some resistance to the wider use of the technology in gaming.Franco says she is already seeing adverts for AI chatbots that let fans talk to their favourite anime characters."I can definitely see AI integrating into games and making it a more realistic experience," she says. "But should that happen I would still see it as just a game. At the end of the day you can't cheat with lines of code."

schema.headline: GTA 6: Can you cheat on someone with a video game character?

title: Tony Pulis column: What Man Utd need now is stability, not more changes
description: Walking into an under-achieving football club is never easy. I know, because I spent my career taking on such challenges.That was the task Michael Car
body: Walking into an under-achieving football club is never easy. I know, because I spent my career taking on such challenges.That was the task Michael Carrick took on in January when he was appointed Manchester United's interim manager and took over a club that was drifting deeper and deeper into mediocrity.Supporters talk about seeing a bounce when new managers take over and, from my own experiences, I do believe that to be the case.Michael certainly experienced a fantastic period where results and performances improved. In his case, United's improvement to finish third and in the Champions League places was exceptional - and he also calmed the water behind the scenes.Yet, with every bounce, there almost always comes a return to normality. You see players who raised the level of their performance return to the level they are used to, and everything often slips back to the way it was before.That seems to be what is happening at United now but, while Carrick appears to be under increasing pressure, the club's problems are definitely not just down to who their manager is.Here, I've tried to explain what he needs to do to sort some of his issues out.To properly judge Michael, you have to balance up everything he has inherited and consider whether United could be a successful organisation.United have invested enormous amounts of money in recruiting a lot of players in the past five years.Since 2021, they have had three other permanent managers - Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, who spent more than £1bn on 27 major signings and many of whom are still at the club.This year, under Michael, they have invested another £150m, but the bulk of it was on three midfielders and if you assess his entire squad I would still seriously question how many players he would have chosen out of the group he now has.As a manager going into troubled clubs, you have to immediately set your non-negotiable principles with your players - things like hard work and a collective spirit in the dressing room were imperative for me.You give everyone the same opportunity to jump on board and then quickly recognise the players who are capable of going on the ride with you, and those who can't, or won't.Michael will know all those things about his squad by now, good and bad, but what can he really do about it?In my experience, and I am talking about Premier League clubs, my owners were keen on my views on the players I had just inherited - not just in terms of their ability on the pitch but their value as assets on budget sheets and in the transfer market.I was always continually asked if I could make players better, and also if I could recover money from those I did not rate or want, so as to help the club's financial position.I understood why - my position as manager was to 100% help the club and try to achieve maximum performances on and off the pitch - but it can be hard to do both.It means when you are taking over a group of players your club has invested in, you cannot always be completely honest about certain players in that group.You know the club has a vested interest in holding the player's value and the fact you have to portray positivity to protect that is sometimes unbelievably difficult.Criticising them in the media can't happen, because of your loyalty to the club, so you are left hoping the people who watch your games week in, week out, understand and recognise your dilemma around your squad.The club's recruitment strategy has been publicly questioned recently, of course, by defender Lisandro Martinez - and I am sure a lot of supporters agree with him and/or would like some clarity on that subject.But, from a manager's perspective, Martinez's outburst also raises serious questions about the player himself.Him saying what he did does make me wonder whether he believes he has been a success personally. If so, then how many more players in United's first-team squad also believe themselves to have been successful, rather than part of the problem?Managing players with inflated opinions about themselves is another challenge in itself - and it certainly needs addressing.You can add that to the list of Michael's issues right now, but he has an even bigger problem in how he deals with his captain Bruno Fernandes' comments after United were humbled by Como in the Champions League on Wednesday,Watching Michael in his post-match press conference in Italy was really difficult for me.I've managed games where my team has been beaten while having a right go, but having to see a manager man up to his side after a performance that, for me, questioned their attitude to compete or even run around and try, was heart-wrenching.Listening to the way his captain spoke, after his own example typified his team's reluctance to do the above, it again showed me how difficult it must be at that club at the moment.Michael's tactics are there to be followed, yet to do that away to Como on a very wet and windy miserable night, you need men and not boys.Fernandes seemed to be enjoying his relationship with Carrick last season, when United were flying up the table, but they have now levelled off both as a team and individuals in the way I described in this column.Proper captains, and I was lucky to work with some top guys, come to the fore when the team and club needs them most.I've always judged leaders by people who follow them when things are going wrong. Unfortunately, many members of that team did follow their captain's example, but in a totally unprofessional way.I don't know Michael well, but he was a very honest player who deservedly has great standing at the club he is now managing.I know his backroom staff better - Steve Holland, Jonny Evans and Jonathan Woodgate - and they are all able assistants with knowledge and experience at the very top level.Whenever United are not winning, there will be calls for things to change - and the manager is almost always at the top of that list.So, where should they look now? I believe they should follow the blueprint of one of their great rivals, and realise that continuously changing direction is just not working.When Mikel Arteta arrived at Arsenal in December 2019, he had an instant impact like Michael - not in terms of league position, but by winning the 2020 FA Cup.For a couple of years after that early success, however, Arteta was taking pelters from fans and across the spectrum of media outlets because the upturn in results did not last.Despite that, the club never flinched and gave him the opportunity to install a clear identity throughout the club and also time for it to take shape. Look where they are now.United have to take their medicine and do similar - they have to understand the consequences of the huge failures in recruitment they have repeatedly made and reset to find a direction and identity again.Time is their biggest challenge there, because everyone demands instant success these days. People, though, have to realise that, while I believe Michael - when everyone is fit - has a group that can still compete for the Champions League places, they are never good enough for the prizes they really want.To be contenders again, they need more than just talent. Ability, pace and character are the characteristics they will need in pretty much every outfield position but, from where they are now, achieving that will not happen quickly.They definitely don't need to change their manager again to get there, however. I was all for Michael getting the job in the first place once Darren Fletcher had been overlooked, and in my humble opinion he should be backed again to do what is needed now.At this moment, United are not capable of winning the league title, whoever is in charge, but stability is the way forward to fix that.Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

schema.headline: Tony Pulis column: What Man Utd need now is stability, not more changes

title: Tottenham Hotspur: Are Roberto de Zerbi's side finally on their way back after win at Chelsea?
description: Whisper it quietly, but could Spurs finally be on their way back?Tottenham's 2-0 win at Chelsea on Saturday moved them up to the heady heights of 12th
body: Whisper it quietly, but could Spurs finally be on their way back?Tottenham's 2-0 win at Chelsea on Saturday moved them up to the heady heights of 12th in the Premier League - their highest league position since 2 January.And, after back-to-back 17th-placed finishes, there are growing signs Roberto de Zerbi's side are showing there is real light at the end of a pretty dark tunnel.Saturday's impressive win at Stamford Bridge was just the second time they have won two league games in a row in 42 attempts - inspired by starring roles from James Maddison and Mathys Tel.It was also the first time they have enjoyed as much as 68% possession in a match since April 2025.The win was deserved too, although Chelsea certainly gave them a helping hand with goalkeeper Mike Penders punching the opener into his own net and Cole Palmer sent off for two yellow cards.Spurs had taken seven attempts to get their first league win of the season against Coventry on Monday and on Saturday they looked transformed from the side that did not even score a goal until September 19.It left De Zerbi glowing with positivity, despite another injury setback for Maddison, as he highlighted a team meeting earlier this month that sparked their revival in fortunes."Seven points after Manchester. Before Manchester we spoke a lot, we had a big meeting," he said. "We removed the masks and spoke honestly and clearly in front of ourselves. From that moment, I think something started to change within us."I think we have put something different into Tottenham in the last period. Not a different attitude, but different relationships with the players, different relationships within the group."We have changed the spirit of the group and improved the performances of the players, especially some of the more fragile players, maybe the younger players. We have suffered enough."Former Chelsea goalkeeper Rob Green added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "A dream afternoon for Tottenham. They looked controlled, looked at ease, they looked like they were comfortable on the ball."Results like this galvanise a side. When you look at the players coming back, yes Maddison got injured and he'll be a question mark over the next few weeks, but players coming back, momentum coming back - you feel, and say it quietly, Tottenham might just be coming back."Italian De Zerbi was appointed Spurs boss at the end of March 2026 with the club in crisis.He arrived as the club's third manager of the campaign and, with seven games remaining, Tottenham were just one point clear of the drop zone.After securing safety, albeit after a few scares, the club spent more than £300m on summer signings for the first time in their history as they backed De Zerbi to restore them to former glories.And, after a slow start to the campaign and still lacking firepower in attack, the long-suffering Tottenham fans will be left feeling more positive than they have done for a long time."Tottenham have made a big statement in a really convincing performance," former Arsenal defender Martin Keown told BBC Sport."I thought Maddison was magnificent in midfield. He's like the Artful Dodger, isn't he? That midfield is full of mischief, but he's brave against the ball."I thought Tel was magnificent out on the left-hand side, [Mohammed] Kudus on the right was also really effective, and everybody really managed to handle the ball really well on the night. "Spurs had almost 70% possession, which is remarkable for a team which was just a few places from the bottom of the table. I think what's changed for Spurs is the key personnel."De Zerbi ran on to the pitch to celebrate with the travelling supporters at the final whistle, while his coaches and substitutes raced towards the players in the corner of the ground.He has previously spoken of how he inherited players that cried after matches and lost all confidence - and believed his unprecedented control over the summer transfers was vindication for Spurs from last season.It was fitting that Tel, who has attracted criticism from his own supporters since signing from Bayern Munich for £30m in June 2025, provided the decisive moment to seal just a second league success in 36 years at Chelsea - a stunning low finish after a driving run.The French forward, 21, told Sky Sports: "It is very special because we have come to Chelsea so many times and not got a win. We showed great mentality today and we need to enjoy this win."We created a lot of chances today. We walk out together, the goal is something special for me, I'm happy about it and let's keep pushing now."Summer signing Matheus Fernandes added: "We are here to change the club's mentality, we want to beat the top teams, and make this victory for the fans."In the summer, Spurs twice broke their transfer record with three of their first signings, as they added centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton, Fernandes from West Ham and Sandro Tonali from Newcastle.And all three impressed De Zerbi against Chelsea as he added: "Jan Paul van Hecke played very well, Matheus Fernandes played very well, Sandro Tonali played very well."I think it was Tonali's best game since joining Tottenham. Omar Marmoush played a good game. It was a tough game for him, but he fought in the right way."Mathys Tel played very well too. I think we won the game with our two wingers, Mohammed Kudus and Mathys Tel. They made the difference."It was notable Fernandes, 22, was criticised by his manager last month.The return of Maddison, who missed almost all of last season with a serious knee injury, was key in Monday's 3-1 home victory over Coventry City - and he again looked impressive before being withdrawn in the second half with a suspected groin injury."I don't think it is a very important problem," said De Zerbi. "I hope it is not a big problem. He is a special player for us. We need him."Maddison is part of a returning group of players, including Kudus and Dejan Kulusevski, who are making comebacks from lengthy absences.Spurs are now unbeaten in three games, with back-to-back victories following the 1-1 draw at Manchester United in which they were arguably the better side.As well as the team meeting before the Old Trafford encounter, Spurs enjoyed a warm-weather training camp in Marbella, where heavyweight boxer Anthony Joshua paid them a visit.It feels as though some semblance of the old Spurs is returning, although they remain unconvincing in attack with just eight goals in as many games.Manchester City loanee Marmoush misfired again and his replacement Dominic Solanke was underwhelming in previous matches, while Richarlison has been frozen out in the reserves after being left out of their Premier League squad.But after this notable derby victory at Chelsea - earning a clean sheet there too for the first time since 1986 - it felt like the first part of De Zerbi's rebuild is well under way.

schema.headline: Tottenham Hotspur: Are Roberto de Zerbi's side finally on their way back after win at Chelsea?

title: Premier League manager 'sacking season' - when is it and who should be worried?
description: While no top-flight manager has been dismissed this season, there are several who will be looking over their shoulder before November's international
body: While no top-flight manager has been dismissed this season, there are several who will be looking over their shoulder before November's international break.The scrutiny on Carrick has only intensified after the chastening 4-1 defeat by Como at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia.Following Lisandro Martinez's critique of the club's hierarchy last week, club captain Bruno Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick's tactics in Como, suggesting all is not well in the Old Trafford dressing room.Asked about Carrick's future after the coach cut an isolated figure as he applauded the away fans alone at full-time, Match of the Day pundit Nedum Onuoha said: "Bruno Fernandes thinks the tactics were essentially wrong in this game, while Michael Carrick thinks the players weren't running enough for the tactics to work out."When you find those sorts of splits it can be very hard within a dressing room to maintain that sort of energy behind the manager."So I think for Carrick himself to go and see those fans... he knows how bad this game was in particular."Tudor's successor at Spurs, Roberto de Zerbi, has eased any pressure on him after successive wins moved them to 12th in the Premier League, while Fulham's Alvaro Arbeloa has also moved the heat away from his future for now with back-to-back 1-0 wins.But new Forest boss Oliver Glasner, and Sunderland's Regis le Bris - whose side are juggling Europa League football - will be feeling a little bit anxious at the moment.Marco Rose, another newcomer to English football, hasn't had the most convincing domestic start with Bournemouth, who face Carrick's United at Old Trafford on Sunday. But surely the midweek win against AC Milan, which extended their perfect Europa League start, is enough to keep the pressure off him for now?Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage apologised to fans after the 5-0 battering by Brighton on Sunday and faces a fight to keep his job only four months after joining from Lens. His side entertain Newcastle on Sunday, another side who's new boss, Matthias Jaissle, could do with a positive result quickly.It may feel early to talk about managers feel the pressure, but history tells us that it might not be long before someone is on their way out.

schema.headline: Premier League manager 'sacking season' - when is it and who should be worried?
